Balta New Jewish Cemetery on Tkachenko Street

Jewish Cemetery · Balta, Ukraine

Not demolished. This cemetery, existing by 1829 per epigraphic data, likely opened after the older Balta cemetery on Bolnychna Street closed, and remains operational today. Jews first settled in Balta in the early 16th century; many suffered the 1768 Haidamak massacre. Population reached 7,364 by 1856, supporting 13 synagogues by mid-century; an 1882 pogrom destroyed 125 Jewish homes and shops. Population reached 13,235 (57%) by 1897, and Balta became a notable Zionist center; peak population of 14,924 (54%) came in 1910, the same year 22 synagogues and two cemeteries operated. A 1916 student Zionist organization, HeKhaver, drew its membership from teachers at the Jewish vocational school. Civil War-era violence, including a nine-day 1919 pogrom by Ukrainian National Republic troops, drove many to flee to Odessa; population fell to 9,116 (40%) by 1926 and 4,711 by 1939. Nazi and Romanian forces occupied Balta on August 5, 1941, establishing a December 1941 ghetto holding about 4,000 Jews (locals and Bessarabian refugees); over 1,000 were deported to Voytovka and Nikolayev, mostly dying of starvation or murder, while orphanage children were sent to Romania. An underground resistance organization with Balta and Odessa members operated throughout the war; 1,795 Balta ghetto Jews survived.
